name: Social Mirror and Embodied Social Presence

mechanism_chain.description: Seeing another person's whole-body movement in architectural space activates mirror neuron circuits (F5, inferior parietal lobule). The simulation is automatic and pre-conscious. Gallese et al. 1996; Rizzolatti et al. 1996.

data.finding: Observation of goal-directed actions activates the same motor circuits (F5 premotor cortex, inferior parietal lobule) as execution of those actions
data.source: Rizzolatti et al. (1996); Gallese et al. (1996)
data.paradigm: Single-cell recording in macaque premotor cortex
data.effect: Mirror neurons fire during action observation

data.finding: Human fMRI confirms homologous mirror system activation during action observation

justification.backing: The mirror neuron system is well-characterized in both non-human primates and humans. Action observation automatically activates motor simulation circuits. Architectural spaces that provide whole-body visibility enable this simulation more fully than spaces that restrict visibility to face-only.
justification.qualifier: The mirror system is primarily demonstrated for hand/arm actions. Whole-body locomotion observation has less direct neural evidence, though the principle of motor simulation extends theoretically.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if action simulation requires attention; but evidence shows mirror activation is automatic and occurs even with divided attention.

mechanism_chain.ceiling_override_rationale: The mechanism or covariance evidence is well-supported and consistent across multiple studies. The confidence exceeds the default warrant ceiling due to replicability, multiple supporting pathways, and/or biological plausibility.

mechanism_chain.description: Embodied simulation generates a phenomenological sense of shared presence — the felt quality of being-with rather than merely being-near. This is Gallese's 'shared manifold': an automatic mapping of the observed person's bodily state onto the observer's motor repertoire.

data.finding: Motor simulation during action observation produces phenomenological resonance — a 'felt sense' of the other's action that constitutes the shared manifold
Second-person neuroscience shows distinct neural signatures for observing vs. being-observed-by another person
data.effect: Interactive social cognition differs from observation

justification.backing: Gallese's shared manifold hypothesis proposes that the mirror system is the neural substrate for embodied intersubjectivity. The automatic mapping of observed action onto own motor repertoire generates the phenomenological sense of 'we-ness' or co-presence.
justification.qualifier: The motor-simulation → phenomenology bridge is philosophically contested. The shared manifold is a theoretical interpretation of the neural data, not a direct observation.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if mirror activation occurs without phenomenological co-presence; some evidence suggests motor simulation can occur without conscious awareness of the other.

competing_accounts.resolution: Panel consensus: simulation and theory-theory may both contribute; Gallese's architectural claims rest on the simulation component

mechanism_chain.description: Embodied co-presence promotes social approach, empathy, and interpersonal coordination. In architectural terms: spaces that support embodied co-presence facilitate prosocial behavior more effectively than spaces that provide only head-and-face visibility.

data.finding: Spaces supporting whole-body visibility (atriums with glass mezzanines, open staircases) produce more spontaneous social interaction than spaces with head-only visibility (high counters, cubicle partitions)
data.effect: Body visibility correlates with social behavior

data.finding: Synchronous movement (enabled by whole-body visibility) enhances cooperation and affiliation

justification.backing: The architectural bridge is that whole-body visibility is a necessary condition for full embodied simulation. Spaces that strip kinematic richness (showing only heads) reduce the motor resonance that underlies social approach and coordination.
justification.qualifier: The direct architectural-to-prosocial link is inferred; controlled studies of architectural visibility and social behavior are limited. The mechanism (simulation → prosociality) is better supported than the architectural modulation.
justification.rebuttal: Would fail if social behavior is determined by factors other than embodied simulation (explicit social norms, task demands); these factors may dominate in many settings.

visual_complexity.source: Gallese & Gattara 2015; Schilbach et al. 2013; panel estimate

open_staircase.note: Movement on stairs is kinematically rich

ie_dpt_interaction: T_IE_011 (Embodiment × Social Space) — motor simulation strength modulated by the observer's own embodied experience of the architectural space

cross_template_interactions.IC2: Body Budget Prediction — embodied co-presence has a dual IC2 signature: motor simulation incurs a small metabolic cost, but the social buffering and anxiety-reduction it provides produces a net IC2 benefit in most non-threatening settings. Threatening social co-presence (co-presence with hostile others) inverts the sign.
cross_template_interactions.AX4: Perceived Control — voluntary exposure to social co-presence (choosing to sit in the atrium vs. the private office) enhances the co-presence benefit. Forced exposure (only communal spaces available, no private alternative) may produce social fatigue.

higher_order_principle: Visual complexity → social setting features pathway: The mechanism by which social mirror and embodied social presence operates
